claim: Toll-6 is expressed in dopaminergic neurons (DANs) in the adult Drosophila brain.
source: We had previously observed that in the adult brain Toll-6 is expressed in dopaminergic neurons (DANs) (McIlroy et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (McIlroy et al., 2013) and confirmed by data in Figure 1I showing co-localization of Toll-6 with TH.

claim: DNT-2 is the ligand for Toll-6 and Kek-6.
source: Here, we focus on Drosophila neurotrophin-2 (DNT-2), proved to be the ligand of Toll-6 and Kek-6, with in vitro, cell culture, and in vivo evidence (McIlroy et al., 2013; Foldi et al., 2017; Ulian-Benitez et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple prior studies providing in vitro, cell culture, and in vivo evidence.

claim: DNT-2A neurons are glutamatergic as they express the vesicular glutamate transporter vGlut.
source: We found that DNT-2A neurons are glutamatergic as they express the vesicular glutamate transporter vGlut (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data showing co-localization of DNT-2 neurons with vGlut marker in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: DNT-2A neurons express the dopamine receptor Dop2R.
source: Using reporters, we found that Dop2R is present in DNT-2A neurons (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: DNT-2A neurons have both pre-synaptic and post-synaptic sites at the SMP and PRW regions.
source: We additionally found post-synaptic signal at the SMP and pre-synaptic signal at the FLA/PRW (Figure 1C, C' and C''), suggesting bidirectional communication at both sites.
evidence: Supported by imaging data showing both DenMark (post-synaptic) and Dsyd1-GFP (pre-synaptic) markers at these locations.

claim: DNT-2A neuron projections show variability across individual flies.
source: Using Multi-Colour Flip-Out (MCFO) to label individual cells stochastically (Nern et al., 2015; Costa et al., 2016), single-neuron clones revealed variability in the DNT-2A projections across individual flies (Figure 1D)
evidence: Supported by MCFO single-cell labeling data in Figure 1D showing different projection patterns.

claim: Toll-6 is expressed in PAM, PPL1, and PPL2 dopaminergic neuron clusters.
source: we found that Toll-6+ neurons included DANs from the PAMs, PPL1, and PPL2 clusters (Figure 1I, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D and F; Supplementary file 1)
evidence: Supported by co-localization data with TH marker shown in Figure 1I and supplementary figures.

claim: Kek-6 is expressed in PAM, PAL, PPL1, PPM2, and PPM3 dopaminergic clusters.
source: Kek-6+ neurons included PAM, PAL, PPL1, PPM2, and PPM3 dopaminergic clusters (Figure 1J, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, E, and F; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by co-localization data with TH marker shown in Figure 1J and supplementary figures.

claim: Toll-6 and kek-6 are expressed in Kenyon cells (KCs).
source: Using MCFO clones revealed that both Toll-6 and kek-6 are also expressed in KCs (Li et al., 2020; Figure 1—figure supplement 2I and J, Supplementary file 1)
evidence: Supported by MCFO clone data in supplementary figures and citation to prior work.

claim: Toll-6 and kek-6 are expressed in DAL neurons.
source: Toll-6 and kek-6 are also expressed in...DAL neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G and H, Supplementary file 1)
evidence: Supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2G and H.

claim: Toll-6 and kek-6 are expressed in mushroom body output neurons (MBONs).
source: Toll-6 and kek-6 are also expressed in...MBONs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: TransTango identified DNT-2A outputs including MB α'β' lobes, αβ KCs, DAL neurons, and dorsal fan-shaped body layer.
source: DNT-2A RFP+ outputs included a subset of MB α'β' lobes, αβ KCs, tip of MB β'2, DAL neurons, dorsal fan-shaped body layer, and possibly PAM or other DANs (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by TransTango connectivity tracing data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: BAcTrace identified PAM-DAN inputs to DNT-2A neurons at SMP.
source: To identify DNT-2A input neurons, we used BAcTrace (Cachero et al., 2020). This identified PAM-DAN inputs at SMP (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by BAcTrace connectivity data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Over-expression of DNT-2FL in DNT-2 neurons increased TH mRNA levels.
source: Using quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR), we found that over-expressing DNT2-FL in DNT-2 neurons in adult flies increased TH mRNA levels in fly heads (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Dop2R RNAi knock-down in DNT-2A neurons significantly increased cAMP levels.
source: Indeed, Dop2R RNAi knock-down in DNT-2A neurons significantly increased cAMP levels (Figure 2D)
evidence: Supported by FRET-based cAMP sensor data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: DNT-2 mutants (DNT237/DNT218) had fewer PAM neurons than controls.
source: Here, we show that DNT237/DNT218 mutant adult brains had fewer PAMs than controls (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by automated cell counting data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Toll-6 RNAi knock-down in DANs decreased PAM neuron number.
source: Similarly, Toll-6 RNAi knock-down in DANs also decreased PAM neuron number (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: DNT-2 mutants had fewer TH+ PAM neurons, which was rescued by over-expressing activated Toll-6CY in DANs.
source: Importantly, PAM cell loss was rescued by over-expressing activated Toll-6CY in DANs in DNT-2 mutants (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by TH immunostaining and cell counting data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Adult-specific DNT-2 RNAi knock-down decreased PAM cell number.
source: Adult-specific DNT-2 RNAi knock-down decreased Tomato+ PAM cell number (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by conditional knock-down and cell counting data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Adult-specific Toll-6 RNAi knock-down in DANs decreased PAM neuron number.
source: Similarly, RNAi Toll-6 knock-down in DANs also decreased PAM neuron number (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by conditional knock-down and cell counting data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Adult-specific DNT-2 RNAi knock-down increased the number of apoptotic cells in the brain.
source: Cell loss was due to cell death as adult-specific DNT-2 RNAi knock-down increased the number of apoptotic cells labelled with anti-Drosophila Cleave caspase-1 (DCP-1) antibodies compared to controls, including Dcp-1+ PAMs and other TH+ cells (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by Dcp-1 immunostaining data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Over-expression of DNT-2FL increased PAM cell number.
source: Instead, and importantly, over-expression of DNT-2FL increased PAM cell number (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: DNT-2 mutants completely lacked DAN synapses in the MB β,β' and γ lobes.
source: Visualising the pre-synaptic reporter Synaptotagmin-GFP (Syt-GFP) in all DANs (with THGal4; R58E02Gal4), we found that DNT-218/DNT-237 mutants completely lacked DAN synapses in the MBβ,β' and γ lobes (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by Syt-GFP reporter imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: DAN connections at α,α' lobes were not affected in DNT-2 mutants.
source: Interestingly, DAN connections at α,α' lobes were not affected (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by Syt-GFP reporter imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Toll-6 RNAi knock-down in PAM β2β'2 neurons decreased dendrite complexity.
source: Toll-6 RNAi knock-down in PAM -β2β'2 (with split-GAL4 MB301BGal4; Aso et al., 2014a) reduced dendrite complexity (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by dendrite morphology analysis data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Over-expression of DNT-2CK in PAM-β2β'2 increased dendrite arbour complexity.
source: Over-expression of DNT-2CK in PAM-β2β'2 increased dendrite arbour complexity (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by dendrite morphology analysis data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: RNAi knock-down of Toll-6, kek-6 or both in PPL1-γped neurons caused axonal terminal misrouting.
source: Using split-GAL4 line MB320C-Gal4 to visualise PPL1 axonal arbours, RNAi knock-down of either Toll-6, kek-6 or both together caused axonal misrouting away from the mushroom body peduncle (Figure 4E and E', chi-square p<0.05, see Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by axonal morphology data shown in Figure 4E and E' with statistical analysis.

claim: DNT-2FL over-expression caused PPL1 axonal misrouting.
source: Similarly, DNT-2FL over-expression also caused PPL1 misrouting (Figure 4F, chi-square p<0.05, see Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by axonal morphology data shown in Figure 4F with statistical analysis.

claim: Adult-specific Toll-6 kek-6 RNAi knock-down in PAM neurons decreased post-synaptic density (PSD) size.
source: Adult-specific Toll-6 kek-6 RNAi knock-down in PAM neurons did not affect synapse number (not shown), but it decreased post-synaptic density (PSD) size, both at the MB lobe and at the SMP dendrite (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by Homer-GCaMP imaging and PSD size analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Neuronal activity increased the number of DNT-2-GFP vesicles produced.
source: We visualised tagged DNT-2FL-GFP in adult brains, activated DNT-2 neurons with TrpA1 at 30°C, and found that DNT-2 neuron activation increased the number of DNT-2-GFP vesicles produced (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Neuronal activity facilitated cleavage of DNT-2 into its mature form.
source: Furthermore, neuronal activity also facilitated cleavage of DNT-2 into its mature form. In western blots from brains over-expressing DNT-2FL-GFP, the levels of full-length DNT-2FL-GFP were reduced following neuronal activation and the cleaved DNT-2CK-GFP form was most abundant (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Activating DNT-2 neurons altered DNT-2 axonal arbours.
source: Activating DNT-2 neurons altered DNT-2 axonal arbours (Figure 5A)
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Activating DNT-2 neurons increased Homer-GFP+ synapse number in the DNT-2 SMP arbour.
source: Activating DNT-2 neurons altered DNT-2 axonal arbours (Figure 5A) and it increased Homer-GFP+ synapse number in the DNT-2 SMP arbour (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by Homer-GFP imaging and synapse counting data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Activating DNT-2 neurons increased the number of Syt+ synapses at the PAM SMP arbour.
source: Activating DNT-2 neurons with TrpA1 increased the number of Syt+ synapses at the PAM SMP arbour (Figure 5C)
evidence: Supported by Syt-GCaMP imaging and synapse counting data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Activating DNT-2 neurons reduced Syt+ synapse size at the PAM SMP arbour.
source: Activating DNT-2 neurons with TrpA1 increased the number of Syt+ synapses at the PAM SMP arbour (Figure 5C) and reduced their size (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by Syt-GCaMP imaging and synapse size analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: DNT-2 neuron activation did not affect synapse number or size at the PAM MB β, β', γ lobes.
source: PAM neurons also send an arborisation at the MB β, β', γ lobes, but DNT-2 neuron activation did not affect synapse number nor size there (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by Syt-GCaMP imaging and analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Over-expression of DNT-2FL in DNT-2 neurons increased Syt+ synapse volume at the PAM SMP dendrite.
source: Over-expression of DNT-2FL in DNT-2 neurons did not alter Syt+ synapse number at the PAM SMP dendrite, but it increased bouton size (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by Syt-GCaMP imaging and synapse size analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Over-expression of DNT-2FL in DNT-2 neurons increased the number of output synapses at the PAM MB β, β' lobe arborisation.
source: In contrast, at the MB β, β' lobe arborisation, over-expressed DNT-2 did not affect Syt+ bouton size, but it increased the number of output synapses (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by Syt-GCaMP imaging and synapse counting data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: DNT-2 mutants had lower climbing ability than controls.
source: We tested the effect of DNT-2 or Toll-6 and kek-6 loss of function in climbing, and both DNT-237/DNT-218 mutants and flies in which DNT-2 was knocked-down in DNT-2 neurons in the adult stage had lower climbing ability than controls (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by startle-induced negative geotaxis assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Adult-specific knock-down of DNT-2 in DNT-2 neurons reduced climbing ability.
source: We tested the effect of DNT-2 or Toll-6 and kek-6 loss of function in climbing, and both DNT-237/DNT-218 mutants and flies in which DNT-2 was knocked-down in DNT-2 neurons in the adult stage had lower climbing ability than controls (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by startle-induced negative geotaxis assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Adult-specific knock-down of Toll-6 and kek-6 in Toll-6 or PAM neurons reduced climbing ability.
source: Similarly, when Toll-6 and kek-6 were knocked-down with RNAi in the adult using a Toll-6- or a PAM-GAL4 neuron driver, climbing was also reduced (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by startle-induced negative geotaxis assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Over-expressing activated Toll-6CY in DANs rescued the locomotion deficits of DNT-2 mutants.
source: Importantly, over-expressing activated Toll-6CY in DANs rescued the locomotion deficits of DNT-2 mutants, showing that DNT-2 functions via Toll-6 in this context (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by climbing assay rescue data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Over-expression of Toll-6CY in DANs increased locomotion in DNT-2 mutants as flies walked longer distances and spent less time immobile.
source: Interestingly, in that setting, locomotion of homozygous DNT-237/DNT-218 mutants was similar to that of controls, but over-expression of Toll-6CY in their DANs increased locomotion as flies walked longer distances and spent less time immobile (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by open arena locomotion tracking data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Adult flies over-expressing DNT2-FL walked faster.
source: Adult flies over-expressing DNT2-FL walked faster (Figure 6E, Figure 5—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by open arena locomotion tracking data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Flies with DNT-2 neurons activated with TrpA1 walked faster.
source: and so did those where DNT-2 neurons were activated with TrpA1 (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by open arena locomotion tracking data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Over-expression of DNT-2FL in DNT-2 neurons in adults enhanced appetitive long-term memory.
source: Remarkably, over-expression of DNT-2FL in DNT-2 neurons in adults enhanced appetitive long-term memory (Figure 6G)
evidence: Supported by appetitive olfactory conditioning data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Both loss and gain of function for DNT-2 caused seizures.
source: Interestingly, both loss and gain of function for DNT-2 also caused seizures (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by bang-sensitivity test data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: DNT-2 and dopamine regulate each other: DNT-2 increased dopamine levels, and in turn dopamine via Dop2R inhibited cAMP signalling in DNT-2A neurons.
source: In summary, DNT-2A neurons are connected to DANs, DAL, and MB KCs, all of which express DNT-2 receptors Toll-6 and kek-6 and belong to a dopaminergic as well as associative learning and memory circuit. Furthermore, DNT-2A and PAM neurons form bidirectional connectivity. Finally, DNT-2 and dopamine regulate each other: DNT-2 increased dopamine levels (Figure 2E), and in turn dopamine via Dop2R inhibited cAMP signalling in DNT-2A neurons (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing DNT-2 increases TH levels (Figure 2C) and FRET data showing Dop2R inhibits cAMP (Figure 2D).

claim: PAM cell number can vary between 220 and 250 cells per Drosophila brain in wild-type flies.
source: In wild-type flies, PAM-DAN number can vary between 220 and 250 cells per Drosophila brain, making them ideal to investigate changes in cell number (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Liu et al., 2012).

claim: Dopamine is required for locomotion, associative reward learning, and long-term memory in Drosophila.
source: Dopamine is required for locomotion, associative reward learning, and long-term memory (Riemensperger et al., 2011; Riemensperger et al., 2013; Waddell, 2013; Sun et al., 2018; Boto et al., 2020; Adel and Griffith, 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: In Drosophila, dopamine-dependent behaviors require PAM, PPL1, and DAL neurons and their connections to KCs and MBONs.
source: In Drosophila, this requires PAM, PPL1, and DAL neurons and their connections to KCs and MBONs (Heisenberg, 2003; Chen et al., 2012; Plaçais et al., 2012; Aso et al., 2014b; Plaçais et al., 2017; Boto et al., 2020; Adel and Griffith, 2021; Huang et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Experience shapes the brain as neural circuits can be modified by neural stimulation or the lack of it.
source: Experience shapes the brain as neural circuits can be modified by neural stimulation or the lack of it.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: Subjective experience requires dopamine, a neuromodulator that assigns a value to stimuli.
source: Subjective experience requires dopamine, a neuromodulator that assigns a value to stimuli, and it also controls behaviour, including locomotion, learning, and memory.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in neuroscience about dopamine's role.

claim: The Drosophila adult brain is plastic and can be modified by experience and neuronal activity.
source: The Drosophila adult brain is plastic and can be modified by experience and neuronal activity (Technau, 1984; Barth and Heisenberg, 1997; Barth et al., 1997; Sachse et al., 2007; Kremer et al., 2010; Sugie et al., 2015; Linneweber et al., 2020; Baltruschat et al., 2021; Çoban et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Toll receptors are expressed across the Drosophila brain in distinct but overlapping patterns that mark anatomical brain domains.
source: Toll receptors are expressed across the Drosophila brain, in distinct but overlapping patterns that mark the anatomical brain domains (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Li et al., 2020).

claim: Tolls share a common signalling pathway downstream that can drive at least four distinct cellular outcomes – cell death, survival, quiescence, and proliferation – depending on context.
source: Tolls share a common signalling pathway downstream that can drive at least four distinct cellular outcomes – cell death, survival, quiescence, and proliferation – depending on context (McIlroy et al., 2013; Foldi et al., 2017; Anthoney et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Mammalian neurotrophins (NTs: BDNF, NGF, NT3, NT4) are growth factors underlying structural brain plasticity.
source: In the mammalian brain, the neurotrophins (NTs: BDNF, NGF, NT3, NT4) are growth factors underlying structural brain plasticity (Poo, 2001; Lu et al., 2005; Park and Poo, 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Mammalian NTs promote neuronal survival, connectivity, neurite growth, synaptogenesis, synaptic plasticity, and long-term potentiation (LTP) via their Trk and p75NTR receptors.
source: They promote neuronal survival, connectivity, neurite growth, synaptogenesis, synaptic plasticity, and long-term potentiation (LTP) via their Trk and p75NTR receptors (Poo, 2001; Lu et al., 2005; Park and Poo, 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: All anti-depressants function by stimulating production of BDNF and signalling via its receptor TrkB, leading to increased brain plasticity.
source: In fact, all anti-depressants function by stimulating production of BDNF and signalling via its receptor TrkB, leading to increased brain plasticity (Casarotto et al., 2021; Castrén and Monteggia, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mammalian NTs have dual functions and can also induce neuronal apoptosis, neurite loss, synapse retraction, and long-term depression (LTD) via p75NTR and Sortilin.
source: Importantly, NTs have dual functions and can also induce neuronal apoptosis, neurite loss, synapse retraction, and long-term depression (LTD) via p75NTR and Sortilin (Lu et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Mammalian TLRs are expressed in all CNS cell types, where they can promote neurogenesis, neurite growth, and synaptogenesis and regulate memory independently of pathogens, cellular damage, or disease.
source: However, mammalian TLRs are expressed in all CNS cell types, where they can promote not only neuroinflammation, but also neurogenesis, neurite growth, and synaptogenesis and regulate memory – independently of pathogens, cellular damage, or disease (Ma et al., 2006; Rolls et al., 2007; Okun et al., 2010; Okun et al., 2011; Patel et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Drosophila Toll receptors can function both independently of ligand-binding and by binding Spätzle (Spz) protein family ligands, also known as Drosophila neurotrophins (DNTs).
source: In Drosophila, Toll receptors can function both independently of ligand-binding and binding Spätzle (Spz) protein family ligands, also known as Drosophila neurotrophins (DNTs), which are sequence, structural, and functional homologues of the mammalian NTs (DeLotto and DeLotto, 1998; Weber et al., 2003; Hoffmann et al., 2008a; Hoffmann et al., 2008b; Zhu et al., 2008; Lewis et al., 2013; McIlroy et al., 2013; Foldi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: DNTs are sequence, structural, and functional homologues of the mammalian NTs.
source: In Drosophila, Toll receptors can function both independently of ligand-binding and binding Spätzle (Spz) protein family ligands, also known as Drosophila neurotrophins (DNTs), which are sequence, structural, and functional homologues of the mammalian NTs (DeLotto and DeLotto, 1998; Weber et al., 2003; Hoffmann et al., 2008a; Hoffmann et al., 2008b; Zhu et al., 2008; Lewis et al., 2013; McIlroy et al., 2013; Foldi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Like mammalian NTs, DNTs also promote cell survival, connectivity, synaptogenesis, and structural synaptic plasticity, and can also promote cell death, depending on context.
source: Like mammalian NTs, DNTs also promote cell survival, connectivity, synaptogenesis, and structural synaptic plasticity, and can also promote cell death, depending on context (Zhu et al., 2008; McIlroy et al., 2013; Sutcliffe et al., 2013; Foldi et al., 2017; Ulian-Benitez et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: DNTs are also ligands for Kekkon (Kek) receptors, kinase-less homologues of the mammalian NT Trk receptors.
source: As well as Tolls, DNTs are also ligands for Kekkon (Kek) receptors, kinase-less homologues of the mammalian NT Trk receptors, and are required for structural synaptic plasticity (Ulian-Benitez et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The targets regulated by Tolls and Keks – ERK, NFκB, PI3K, JNK, CaMKII – are shared with those of mammalian NT receptors Trk and p75NTR.
source: Importantly, the targets regulated by Tolls and Keks – ERK, NFκB, PI3K, JNK, CaMKII – are shared with those of mammalian NT receptors Trk and p75NTR, and have key roles in structural and functional plasticity across the animals (Park and Poo, 2013; Foldi et al., 2017; Ulian-Benitez et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2020; Tamada et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: A feedback loop involving dopamine and DNT-2 highlighted the circuits engaged, and DNT-2 with Toll-6 and Kek-6 induced structural plasticity in this circuit modifying brain function and behaviour.
source: To conclude, a feedback loop involving dopamine and DNT-2 highlighted the circuits engaged, and DNT-2 with Toll-6 and Kek-6 induced structural plasticity in this circuit modifying brain function and behaviour.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: DNT-2FL is spontaneously cleaved into the mature form.
source: Importantly, DNT-2FL is spontaneously cleaved into the mature form (McIlroy et al., 2013; Foldi et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work and western blot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: DNT-2FL enables investigation of non-autonomous functions of DNT-2.
source: Importantly, over-expressing DNT-2FL enables to investigate non-autonomous functions of DNT-2 (Ulian-Benitez et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: DNT-2CK is not secreted from transfected S2 cells, but it is functional in vivo.
source: DNT-2CK is not secreted (from transfected S2 cells), but it is functional in vivo (Zhu et al., 2008; Foldi et al., 2017; Ulian-Benitez et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Over-expressed DNT-2CK functions cell-autonomously, whereas DNT-2FL functions also non-autonomously, but they have similar effects.
source: Importantly, over-expressed DNT-2CK functions cell-autonomously, whereas DNT-2FL functions also non-autonomously, but they have similar effects (Zhu et al., 2008; Foldi et al., 2017; Ulian-Benitez et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: DNT-2 is a retrograde factor at the larval NMJ, where transcripts are located post-synaptically in the muscle, and DNT-2FL-GFP is taken up from muscle by motoneurons, where it induces synaptogenesis.
source: Similarly, DNT-2 is a retrograde factor at the larval NMJ, where transcripts are located post-synaptically in the muscle, and DNT-2FL-GFP is taken up from muscle by motoneurons, where it induces synaptogenesis (Sutcliffe et al., 2013; Ulian-Benitez et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In mammals, neuronal activity induces synthesis, release, and cleavage of BDNF, leading to neuronal survival, dendrite growth and branching, synaptogenesis, and synaptic plasticity (i.e. LTP).
source: In mammals, neuronal activity induces synthesis, release, and cleavage of BDNF, leading to neuronal survival, dendrite growth and branching, synaptogenesis, and synaptic plasticity (i.e. LTP) (Poo, 2001; Horch and Katz, 2002; Lu et al., 2005; Arikkath, 2012; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Mammalian BDNF increases synapse number, spine size, and LTP, but it can also regulate homeostatic plasticity and LTD, depending on the timing, levels, and site of action.
source: Mammalian BDNF increases synapse number, spine size, and LTP, but it can also regulate homeostatic plasticity and LTD, depending on the timing, levels, and site of action (Poo, 2001; Lu et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Mammalian NTs promote dopamine release and the expression of DA receptors.
source: Similarly, mammalian NTs also promote dopamine release and the expression of DA receptors (Blöchl and Sirrenberg, 1996; Guillin et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: DAN cell survival is maintained by NT signalling in mammals and fish.
source: Furthermore, DAN cell survival is maintained by DNT-2 in Drosophila, and similarly DAN cell survival is also maintained by NT signalling in mammals and fish (Hyman et al., 1991; Sahu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Alterations in both NTs and dopamine underlie many psychiatric disorders and neurodegenerative diseases in humans.
source: Importantly, alterations in both NTs and dopamine underlie many psychiatric disorders and neurodegenerative diseases in humans (Hyman et al., 1991; Guillin et al., 2001; Berton et al., 2006; Forrest et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: In humans, structural brain plasticity (e.g. adult neurogenesis, neuronal survival, neurite growth, and synaptogenesis) correlates with anti-depressant treatment, learning, physical exercise, and well-being.
source: Importantly, in humans, structural brain plasticity (e.g. adult neurogenesis, neuronal survival, neurite growth, and synaptogenesis) correlates with anti-depressant treatment, learning, physical exercise, and well-being (Cotman and Berchtold, 2002; Woollett and Maguire, 2011; Castrén and Monteggia, 2021; Cheng et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Neurite, synapse, and cell loss correlate with ageing, neuroinflammation, psychiatric, and neurodegenerative conditions.
source: Conversely, neurite, synapse, and cell loss correlate with ageing, neuroinflammation, psychiatric, and neurodegenerative conditions (Holtmaat and Svoboda, 2009; Lu et al., 2013; Wohleb et al., 2016; Forrest et al., 2018; Vahid-Ansari and Albert, 2021; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.
